Pulsed beeps play in one ear at a time, 500 Hz to 8 kHz. One statistical model of your thresholds covers every band and both ears: each beep plays at the level that teaches it most, and a band ends once its threshold is known well enough. Silent beeps measure guessing. About 2 minutes instead of 6.
From the listening check to EQ

Your thresholds are compared with a reference listener\'s on well-tuned headphones of your type (ISO 389-7, Harman target). PureEQ corrects the smooth trend from your low mids (500 Hz to 1.5 kHz), and only what the answers clearly show: small differences at 75 %, larger ones at about a third. Bass below 400 Hz is left to your taste, treble boosts stop at +6 dB, and the ears differ only where the answers clearly show it.

Optionally, pick your model from AutoEq\'s database (over 6,000 headphones measured by oratory1990, crinacle, Rtings and others). PureEQ corrects its measurement to the Harman target the way AutoEq does: smoothed, with gentle slopes, boosts up to +6 dB, and half strength above 5 kHz, where ears differ most. The listening check then only fixes your ears and the fit.

The EQ\'s total bass is kept within what it\'s worth. Over-ear headphones hold bass below 50 Hz near the 50 Hz level, since a boost there costs as much volume; Full sub-bass in Fine-tune lifts this. No headphones get more than +12 dB (over-ear) or +15 dB (in-ear) of bass over the mids.

Bass (a 105 Hz shelf) and treble (a broad shelf from 2.5 kHz) are tuned by blind A/B pairs, loudness-matched (ITU BS.1770) so louder never wins. PureEQ starts from Harman\'s three groups of listeners, learns from every answer, \"Same\" included, and picks each next pair to learn the most: usually 5 to 7 rounds. Air, warmth and vocals are yours to set.

Ears lose bass faster than mids as sound gets quieter (ISO 226). Below the volume of your taste test, the system-wide EQ adds back half of that loss: about 1.5 dB of bass at 105 Hz for every 10 dB quieter, up to +6 dB, and up to +2 dB of treble. It follows the volume keys, and Fine-tune has the switch.

Each profile is tuned for what its headphones are mostly for; switch any time. A mode reshapes your tuning, shapes both ears alike and plays as loud as Music. Music: exactly as tuned. General: +1.5 dB around 2.5 kHz and a slow leveller (2:1, 3 s release). Gaming: bass at −3 dB or less, +2 dB at 2 kHz, treble never cut, and about 21 ms of delay instead of 43. Voice: less boom below 100 Hz, +2.5 dB at 2 kHz, full ear tuning and a leveller (2:1, 0.4 s release). Levellers only turn down. Android keeps calls and low-latency games away from every app\'s effects.

Auto goes by what each app says it\'s playing, which Android tells every app (but not which app it is): a game plays as Gaming, speech as Voice, music as Music, films and a mix as General, and anything unnamed as Music. It switches once something new has played for 3 s; pauses change nothing. Most games don\'t say they\'re games, so pick Gaming for them.

PureEQ keeps on or off for each output; the phone speaker starts off. \"All audio\" uses Android\'s DynamicsProcessing on the output mix, with a curve for each ear in fine bands (each FFT bin in the bass, 1/16 octave above). The level drops only as much as the music needs. Exports use AutoEq\'s formats, read by Wavelet, Poweramp Equalizer, JamesDSP and Equalizer APO.

Profiles and results stay on this phone, and in Android\'s encrypted backup if it\'s on. The room check listens for 3 seconds and stores nothing. PureEQ goes online only to check for its own updates and, if you look up your headphones, to download AutoEq\'s public data from jsDelivr or GitHub. Nothing about you is sent.
